spec.full_target:
Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
\(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.

Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
spec.conclusion: dim_H(E×[0,1])=dim_H(E)+1, with E×[0,1]=F in the Euclidean space Eucl(n+1).

definitions.type: family, indexed by k∈ℕ, of Euclidean metric spaces
definitions.definition: Eucl(k)=ℝ^k, the real coordinate vectors indexed by {0,...,k−1}, with distance dist(x,y)=(∑_{j<k}(x_j−y_j)^2)^(1/2). Eucl(0) consists of the empty vector. On Eucl(k)×ℝ we use dist((x,t),(y,u))=(dist(x,y)^2+|t−u|^2)^(1/2), identified with Eucl(k+1) by appending the last coordinate; no maximum product metric is used. Balls mean {y:dist(x,y)<a}. All these spaces carry the topology of this metric and its Borel measurable structure.

definitions.type: extended nonnegative diameter of a subset of a metric or extended metric space
definitions.definition: For a subset A of a metric or extended metric space X, diam(A)=sup{d(x,y):x,y∈A} in [0,∞], where d is its (extended) distance and sup∅=0. Thus diam∅=0. When diam(A)≤a<∞ we treat it as the corresponding finite nonnegative real number. Countable sums of nonnegative quantities mean the supremum of finite partial sums, and may be infinite; powers with positive exponent have 0^s=0 and ∞^s=∞.

definitions.type: Hausdorff content and measure functions on Euclidean sets with positive real exponent
definitions.definition: For every k∈ℕ, A⊆Eucl(k), s>0 and δ>0, H^s_δ(A)=inf{∑_{i≥0}(diam U_i)^s : (U_i) is a countable cover of A and diam U_i≤δ for every i}, and H^s(A)=sup_{δ>0} H^s_δ(A), with values in [0,∞]. Finite covers are allowed by padding with empty sets; empty members contribute zero. The infimum of an empty collection is ∞. This is exactly the unnormalized diameter-power convention of problem.md:34–42.

definitions.type: pair of native Hausdorff measure and dimension constructions on an extended metric space
definitions.definition: For an extended metric space X with its Borel measurable structure, Native(X).measure(σ) denotes MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure σ, defined in the pinned library as Measure.mkMetric(r↦r^σ). Here mkMetric forms, for each positive extended radius, the covering outer measure with cost r^σ of the extended diameter for nonempty sets (empty sets cost zero), and takes their supremum as the radius decreases to zero, with the Borel measure structure. Evaluations on arbitrary sets mean outer measure evaluations, without requiring those sets measurable. Extended powers use the native ENNReal.rpow convention, including r^0=1. Native(X).dimension(A) denotes dimH A, defined as sup over a∈[0,∞) with Native(X).measure(a)(A)=∞ of the extended nonnegative number a; an empty supremum is zero. This names the exact native definitions, not an assertion about H.

binders.type: extended metric space with its Borel measurable structure

definitions.type: extended nonnegative Hausdorff dimension of Euclidean sets
definitions.definition: For k∈ℕ and A⊆Eucl(k), dim_H(A)=Native(Eucl(k)).dimension(A), the usual Hausdorff dimension, valued in [0,∞]. In particular the empty set has dimension zero by this definition. No finiteness is imposed by this definition; finiteness of the dimensions occurring in the target is proved below.
F=E×I={(x,t):x∈E,t∈I}, regarded as a subset of Eucl(n+1) under D001's coordinate-appending Euclidean isometry.
D=dim_H(E). Finiteness and 0≤D≤n are conclusions, not assumptions.

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure on the Borel real line, evaluated as an outer measure on arbitrary sets
definitions.definition: λ is the usual Lebesgue measure MeasureTheory.volume on ℝ. For any nonnegative extended-real function f, ∫f dλ denotes its nonnegative Lebesgue integral (the supremum of the integrals of nonnegative measurable simple functions bounded above by f). For a set B and constant c≥0, c 1_B is c on B and zero outside B. For a bounded open interval J=(a,b) with a<b its length |J| means b−a.

locals.declaration: Fix an arbitrary k∈ℕ.
Fix an arbitrary A⊆Eucl(k).
Fix an arbitrary real s; for the following conditional argument assume s>0.
Let δ>0 be arbitrary, locally under the positive-scale condition.
Let L>0 be arbitrary.

At each finite positive radius r consider any countable cover U admissible at r.

argument.text: Fix k,A,s as declared and temporarily assume L1: s>0. Apply M001 to X=Eucl(k), σ=s and the current A. Its Borel structure is the one fixed in D001. At a finite positive radius the summand for an empty member is zero and that for a nonempty member is (diam U_i)^s; this also vanishes on a singleton because s>0. Thus the inner infimum is precisely H^s_r(A). The radius ∞ contributes no larger value than the radius 1, since every cover admissible at 1 is admissible at ∞. Hence allowing extended radii does not enlarge the supremum over finite positive radii. Finite or other countable covers can be enumerated and padded by empty members, preserving every cost. M001 therefore gives H^s(A)=Native(Eucl(k)).measure(s)(A).

The dimension in D005 is exactly the native dimension, and is nonnegative since it takes values in [0,∞]. Under s>0, s defines a nonnegative real source exponent. Apply M002 when s<dim_H(A) to obtain native measure ∞, and apply M003 when dim_H(A)<s to obtain native measure zero. In both cases F001 identifies this value with H^s(A). If H^s(A)=0, F001 makes the native measure different from ∞, so M004 gives dim_H(A)≤s. If H^s(A)=∞, F001 and M005 give s≤dim_H(A). Each conditional source use retains exactly its antecedent; no conclusion is asserted without that antecedent.

produces.statement: dim_H(A)≥0; if s>dim_H(A) then H^s(A)=0; if 0<s<dim_H(A) then H^s(A)=∞; if H^s(A)=0 then dim_H(A)≤s; and if H^s(A)=∞ then dim_H(A)≥s.

argument.text: For positive δ, decreasing δ restricts the admissible covers and therefore increases their infimum. All costs are nonnegative. If H^s(A)=0, every scale infimum is zero. By the defining greatest-lower-bound property, for every positive threshold a cover has cost below it: otherwise that positive threshold would be a lower bound. If H^s(A)=∞, its defining supremum supplies a scale with content>L for every finite L>0. Replacing that scale by its minimum with δ0 preserves this strict inequality and gives a scale no larger than δ0. These are implications for arbitrary positive L,δ0,δ. Discharge L1 and universally quantify k,A,s with its positivity condition, obtaining the exported conclusion.

locals.declaration: At the current positive δ, choose the finite centers T whose radius-δ/2 balls cover E, supplied by F002.
Fix an arbitrary 0<h≤1 in the mesh argument.
Define C=(2R+1)^n, independent of h.

argument.text: H002 and M012 imply that E is bounded in the Euclidean metric bornology. In Euclidean space, a bounded set has its distances from the origin bounded by a finite constant; increasing that bound to a positive number bounds each absolute coordinate of every x∈E, because for every coordinate j<n, |x_j|≤(∑_{j<n}|x_j|^2)^(1/2). Thus there exists R>0 such that E⊆[−R,R]^n. This interpretation uses precisely the metric bornology, whose bounded sets lie in some finite-radius ball.

Choose R from F001. For arbitrary s>0,δ>0, cover E by the open balls of radius δ/2 centered at every point of Eucl(n). They cover since each point belongs to its own ball. Each ball is open in D001's metric topology, and its diameter is≤δ by the triangle inequality. H002 and M013 supply a finite subcover. Thus a finite ball-cover with these diameters exists for every positive δ.

produces.statement: For every δ′>0 there is a finite set T′⊆Eucl(n) such that the balls with centers in T′ and radius δ′/2 cover E and have diameter≤δ′.

argument.text: For each positive s and δ in F002, choose its finite subcover T. Each ball's s-cost is≤δ^s, so the finite cost sum is finite. The infimum H^s_δ(E) is no greater than that cost, and is therefore finite. This proves the universally quantified finite-cover and content clauses in the exported conclusion.

produces.statement: For every s′>0 and δ′>0, E has a finite ball-cover of diameter≤δ′ with finite total s′-cost, and H^s′_δ′(E)<∞.

argument.text: First assume L1: n≥1. For 0<h≤1 partition each coordinate interval [−R,R] into at most ceil(2R/h) closed subintervals of length≤h. Their products cover the box and hence E. The number of cubes (possibly shorter at the boundary) is≤(2R/h+1)^n≤C h^(−n), where C=(2R+1)^n depends only on the fixed box. Each diameter is≤√n h by summing the squared coordinate differences. For s>n the total s-cost is≤C n^(s/2) h^(s−n), which tends to zero as h↓0 by M015 with y=s−n>0 and source variable 1/h; the factor C n^(s/2) is fixed and finite. For any fixed target scale, h can be arbitrarily small while √n h is below it; hence every scale content is zero and H^s(E)=0. N001 gives D≤s for every s>n. It follows that D≤n: if D>n, choose a finite real s strictly between n and D (also possible if D=∞), contradicting D≤s. Discharge L1. In the remaining case L2: n=0, Eucl(0) has only the empty vector; H001 implies E=Eucl(0). Its singleton cover has zero s-cost for every s>0, so N001 gives D≤s for every positive s, whence D=0. Discharge L2. Nonnegativity in both cases is N001, giving 0≤D≤n and all the remaining clauses of the exported conclusion.

M016 and M017 therefore give a real least upper bound and a real greatest lower bound of B. Each is unique by order antisymmetry; denote them sup B and inf B. For every b'∈B, all b∈B satisfy b≤b'+ρ; the least-upper-bound property gives sup B≤b'+ρ. Thus sup B−ρ is a lower bound for B, so the greatest-lower-bound property gives sup B−ρ≤inf B. Therefore sup B−inf B≤ρ, including ρ=0.

For any a>1, the N equal closed pieces of I therefore give a cover of F of maximum diameter 1/N and total a-cost N(1/N)^a=N^(1−a)→0 as N→∞ by M015 with y=a−1>0 (restricting the real variable to positive integers). argument.text: Assume L2: n≥1, q>D, 0<r≤1, and ε>0. N002 gives D≥0, so q>0. N001 gives H^q(E)=0 and an r-cover U0 of q-cost<ε/2. Discard empty members. Each zero-diameter nonempty member is a singleton, since all its pairwise distances vanish. Replace its member at original index i by an open ball about that point of positive diameter≤r and q-cost<ε 2^(−i−2). Such balls exist in Eucl(n) because n≥1: a radius smaller than both r/2 and (ε 2^(−i−2))^(1/q)/2 works, and the ball has positive diameter. Leave positive-diameter members unchanged. Countable choice makes these replacements simultaneously. The added cost is bounded by ∑_{i≥0} ε 2^(−i−2)=ε/2, so the resulting cover has positive diameters≤r and cost<ε. Since 0<r_i≤1, N_i≥1, 1/N_i≤r_i and N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i. The W form a countable cover of F: first cover the E coordinate by U_i, then partition I in the corresponding i-th fiber. Two points of the same W differ by≤r_i horizontally and≤r_i vertically, so their Euclidean distance is≤√2 r_i. Therefore ∑_{i,j} diam(W_(i,j))^(q+1) ≤ ∑_i N_i(√2 r_i)^(q+1) ≤2(√2)^(q+1)∑_i r_i^q <2(√2)^(q+1)ε. Regrouping is valid for nonnegative series, defined as suprema of finite sums. argument.text: Assume L4: n≥1 and q>D. For any δ>0 define r_*=min(1,δ/√2)>0 and apply F003 with its scale argument equal to r_*. For every ε>0 the resulting cover is admissible at δ and has (q+1)-cost<2(√2)^(q+1)ε. The coefficient is positive and finite, so these costs can be smaller than any positive threshold. Nonnegativity of the infimum implies H^(q+1)_δ(F)=0. Since δ was arbitrary, taking the supremum gives H^(q+1)(F)=0. N001, with positive exponent q+1, gives dim_H(F)≤q+1. argument.text: By N002, D is finite. In the n≥1 case, F004 gives dim_H(F)≤q+1 for every q>D. One such q first makes dim_H(F) finite. If dim_H(F)>D+1, a q strictly between D and dim_H(F)−1 contradicts that inequality; hence dim_H(F)≤D+1. This is the limit q↓D without assuming a measure statement at the critical exponent. argument.text: Fix 0<s<1 and δ>0. For every 0≤ρ≤δ, ρ^s≥δ^(s−1)ρ: if ρ=0 both sides are zero, and otherwise ρ^(s−1)≥δ^(s−1) since s−1<0. For 0<s<1, F003 therefore gives H^s(A)=∞ and N001 gives dim_H(A)≥s; the strict-between argument yields dim_H(A)≥1. argument.text: Assume L1: D>0. By N002, D is finite. For every 0<s<D, N001 gives H^s(E)=∞. N005 gives H^s_δ(E)≤H^(s+1)_δ(F) for every δ>0. Taking the supremum over δ gives ∞=H^s(E)≤H^(s+1)(F), so H^(s+1)(F)=∞. Equivalently, the arbitrarily large small-scale contents provided by N001 transfer directly through N005. Applying N001 to F at exponent s+1>0 yields dim_H(F)≥s+1. Let s↑D: if dim_H(F)<D+1, choose 0<s<D with s>dim_H(F)−1, possible since D>0 and the strict inequality holds; this contradicts dim_H(F)≥s+1. Thus dim_H(F)≥D+1 under L1. Discharge L1.

Assume L2: D=0. H001 provides x0∈E; define e:I→Eucl(n+1) by e(t)=(x0,t). By D007 its image lies in F. By D001, dist(e(t),e(u))=sqrt(dist(x0,x0)^2+|t−u|^2)=|t−u| for all t,u∈I. Thus N006 applies with k=n+1 and A=F and gives dim_H(F)≥1. Since D=0, this is dim_H(F)≥D+1. This argument includes n=0 and requires no positive-diameter balls in Eucl(0). Discharge L2.

N002 gives D≥0, hence either D>0 or D=0. F001 and F002 yield dim_H(F)≥D+1 in all cases. N004 gives the matching upper bound. Antisymmetry implies dim_H(F)=D+1. Substituting D=dim_H(E), I=[0,1] and F=E×I under the Euclidean coordinate identification gives exactly dim_H(E×[0,1])=dim_H(E)+1 in Eucl(n+1), which is P.
